title: What the Wall Takes
passage:
The last property on the new run is a bungalow at the head of a lane, and the fitting Wesley Crowdleigh wants is under the sink. He stands a dilution box on the draining board, opens its needle valve a quarter-turn at a time and sniffs at the funnel until the smell arrives. The box counts in parts of gas to a thousand parts of air: the figure he writes down is the fraction he needs in front of him before he can smell anything. At the first house on this run the figure was three. Here it is eleven. He is working to four, a fifth of the leanest mixture of propane and air that will burn. Nothing has ever gone wrong on this lane. The vessel at the bottom of it was filled three weeks ago, every joint was pressure-tested, the paperwork is signed, and the twenty-six houses above it are due to be lit on Thursday.

Propane leaves the refinery with no smell on it. What warns you at a cooker is ethyl mercaptan, a sulphur compound put into the gas at the depot at a fixed weight to a fixed volume. The warning is not a property of the fuel. It is a coating on it, a passenger, and passengers can get off. The inside of a new steel main is not the smooth tube it looks: it carries mill scale from the rolling and a bloom of rust from the weeks the lengths stood in the yard, and that oxide is rough and chemically hungry. Some of the mercaptan simply sticks to it. Some is oxidised on contact into a disulphide, a serviceable molecule that is no use as a warning, because it hardly smells. Either way the gas that leaves the far end has less smell in it than the gas that went in, and the further it has travelled against that wall, the less it has.

Crowdleigh’s sheet reads like a slope: three at the cottage nearest the vessel, five at the farm office halfway up, eleven at the bungalow. The slope is not a fault in the pipe and it is not a fault in the fill. It is the wall taking its share, house by house, and taking more the longer the run gets. What decides how much it takes runs against a householder’s intuition. Bare oxide takes the most, so a main scrubs hardest in the week it goes into service; a wide bore takes more than a narrow one; and slow gas gives up more than fast gas, which on a new estate makes it worse. Age works the other way about. Once a stretch of wall has taken all it can hold it stops taking, and the gas goes past unchanged. The old steel line that has fed the farm buildings since the sixties is longer than the new run, is the same bore, comes off the same vessel and the same fill, and reads three at both ends. The buried plastic that replaced most of the country’s old iron takes almost none of it. The pipe that needs watching is the pipe nobody has ever used.

The remedy is called pickling, and it has a bill. You saturate the wall on purpose, holding the system at three or four times the ordinary dose until it will take no more, and you do it before the first burner is lit. On a run this size that means several days of gas, an unbudgeted tanker movement, and a fortnight in which a village that has never smelled gas smells gas. Crowdleigh warns the parish council first; one call-out to a kitchen where the cooker is off and the smell is only the soak costs more than the odorant does. What he cannot do is put a date on the end of it in advance. The soak ends when the readings say it has ended, which means walking the run again. “The box is honest about the dilution and silent about the nose,” he says. “That eleven is eleven to me, this morning, with no cold. It isn’t a reading off the gas. I can’t hand you the figure the chap in the bungalow would have got, and he’s the one who has to smell it in the small hours.”

The heavy dose went into the vessel on Monday and the run has been held at it since. Thursday has moved to the Thursday after. Crowdleigh is out on the lane again, working down from the top this time, at the third kitchen of the morning: units pulled out, floor up, the cooker still capped. He opens the needle valve a quarter-turn at a time. The figure he writes down is six.
– Rosemary Vipond

questions.prompt: What are we told about the numbers Crowdleigh writes down?

questions.rationale:
C is right. The box lets gas into clean air a little at a time until the smell arrives, and “the figure he writes down is the fraction he needs in front of him before he can smell anything”. Eleven at the bungalow means he needed almost four times as much gas in front of him as at the cottage, where the figure was three.

A turns the scale the wrong way up. A larger figure means more gas is needed before the smell gets through, so the sheet runs “three at the cottage nearest the vessel, five at the farm office halfway up, eleven at the bungalow” as the warning gets weaker, and eleven is the figure that stops the lighting-up.

B keeps the procedure and drops the measurement. The quarter-turns are how he gets there; what goes on the sheet is a fraction of gas in air, because “The box counts in parts of gas to a thousand parts of air”.

D makes the figure a calculation instead of a reading. The older line settles that: it “is longer than the new run” and still “reads three at both ends”, so distance does not set the number.

questions.rationale:
A is right. The wall does two things, and the second is the one that costs the warning: “Some of the mercaptan simply sticks to it. Some is oxidised on contact into a disulphide, a serviceable molecule that is no use as a warning, because it hardly smells”. The sulphur is still in the gas; the smell is not.

B moves the dosing to the estate. The passage puts it somewhere else, and at a set rate: the compound is “put into the gas at the depot at a fixed weight to a fixed volume”, which is why the first house on the new run reads three before anybody at the estate has touched it.

C ties the loss to corrosion in service, which is what a householder expects and the wrong way round. The oxide is on the steel before the main carries anything: it “carries mill scale from the rolling and a bloom of rust from the weeks the lengths stood in the yard”.

D moves the loss indoors. The passage puts it in transit: “the gas that leaves the far end has less smell in it than the gas that went in, and the further it has travelled against that wall, the less it has”.

questions.prompt: What is implied about the date set for lighting the houses?

It has slipped by a week, with the heavy dose still held in the run.

questions.rationale:
D is right. The last paragraph moves the date by exactly a week: “Thursday has moved to the Thursday after”. What the date has moved for is standing in the run – “The heavy dose went into the vessel on Monday and the run has been held at it since” – so the houses wait on a soak instead of being lit.

A keeps the first date, with the heavy dose fitted into the weeks in front of it. Neither half survives: the date moves, and the end of a soak cannot be booked in advance, because “What he cannot do is put a date on the end of it in advance”.

B leaves the job open-ended. A new date is named, a week after the first, so the lighting-up has been put back rather than given up; and the council hears from Crowdleigh at the start, since he “warns the parish council first”.

generator_meta.mechanism_verification_note: Verified against the literature before drafting, and one framing was corrected by the check. (1) SUBSTRATE: the adsorption and the odorant-destroying reaction happen on the IRON OXIDE layer - mill scale and rust - inside new STEEL pipe and new steel vessels. Mercaptan adsorbs on that oxide and part of it is oxidised to a disulphide, which is far less odorous. Polyethylene is the material that REDUCES the problem, and the passage says so in one sentence rather than building the piece on it. A polyethylene framing would have failed verification. (2) DIRECTION OF THE FACTORS: adsorption rises with rust area, pressure and temperature and falls with flow rate and with odorant concentration, so the worst case is a long, large-bore, freshly laid, low-flow run. The passage carries three of those (bare oxide, wide bore, slow gas) and does not assert the two it does not use. (3) SATURATION: pre-odorisation, called pickling, saturates the wall by running the line at a deliberately elevated odorant dose until tail-end odorant levels hold steady and match the inlet, which is exactly the passage's stopping rule (a second walk, not a date). (4) THRESHOLD ARITHMETIC: the code requirement is that the odorant be detectable at one-fifth of the lower explosive limit. Propane's LEL is about 2.1 per cent by volume in air, so one-fifth of it is about 0.42 per cent, which is about four parts of gas in a thousand of air. The passage's working figure of four, and its readings of three, five, six and eleven on the same scale, are arithmetically consistent with that and were checked rather than invented. (5) ODORANT: ethyl mercaptan is the standard LPG odorant (commonly blended with dimethyl sulphide), which is why the passage names it rather than the tetrahydrothiophene used in mains natural gas.

B moves the loss to the outlet, when it happens along the pipe, which is why the readings climb with distance: “three at the cottage nearest the vessel, five at the farm office halfway up, eleven at the bungalow”.

C lights most of the houses on time. The passage sets one date for the whole run: “the twenty-six houses above it are due to be lit on Thursday”. It is that single date which moves, and not one house is held back from the lighting-up.
